title: Shares of Global FX Reserves — the dollar, the euro, the yen, sterling and the franc
date: Data vintage: IMF COFER annual through 2025 · annual, 1980–2025
standfirst: Japan Macro Advisors' estimates of the currency composition of world foreign exchange reserves, annual from 1980. Each currency is shown as the IMF publishes it, as we extend it back, and with exchange-rate movements stripped out.
stamp: Data vintage: IMF COFER annual through 2025. The constant-rate series is valued at end-2025 exchange rates.
intro_html: The IMF publishes the currency composition of world reserves in COFER, but only from 1995. These pages carry our own series, which extends the record back to 1980, alongside the published one.
bottom_banner: The charts and data on this page are free to use and reproduce with attribution to Japan Macro Advisors. This page is shared with paid subscribers. The series are updated once a year, when the IMF closes its COFER year.
_note: Standing dataset, not an article panel. Every value is cut from the accepted research artifacts — reserve-share-unadjusted-1975-2025-v10.csv (the observed panel), cer-v4/ (the constant-exchange-rate build) and cofer-annual-full-2026-07-27.csv (COFER as published) — never re-derived from a pipeline run. Chart form ruled by Takuji 2026-08-05: one chart per currency carrying all three measures, rather than one chart per measure carrying all three currencies. Levels and flows are published to one decimal, the precision the pre-2000 printed sources support; exhibit 10 draws only on COFER-era data and is shown to two. Rounding is half away from zero, the convention published statistics use — Python's default is half-to-even, which printed 1998 as 66.2 and made the About block's stated 0.6 gap to the Annual Report read as 0.5. A QA gate now holds that figure. The euro begins in 2000 (2001 for the flow) by Takuji's ruling of 2026-08-05: before the single currency, euro-area reserves were held in the mark, franc and guilder, and combining them involves conventions this page keeps out; the COFER line on that chart begins in 1999, its own first euro year. Deliberately absent: years before 1980, every currency outside the five, the unattributed residual as its own series, and the allocation-estimate research. Sterling and the Swiss franc were added 2026-08-07 on Takuji's ruling of 2026-08-05, both from 1980 and given the same treatment as the dollar and the yen; their flow charts were added the same day on Takuji's ruling, reversing the work order's instruction to publish their flow columns in the download alone. Every currency the page charts now has a flow chart except the euro, whose flow begins only in 2001.

about.heading: Our estimation method
about.lead: This is the methodology note on how we extended the COFER statistics back toward 1980.

blocks.text: Our statistics are based on Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER), published by the IMF and starting in 1995. The IMF publishes its estimates of the currency composition of FX reserves, but its estimate only applies to 2000-2025. Between 1995 and 1999, a significant part of FX reserves is “unallocated”. Our series extends the statistics back, drawing on the currency-composition tables in successive editions of the IMF's Annual Reports, supplemented by BIS statistics and national central-bank disclosures.
Our statistics differ from IMF COFER in the following key aspects.

blocks.head: 1) Reattributing ECUs as USD.
blocks.text: Before the arrival of the euro, European central banks held ECUs, claims backed by gold and US dollars, as part of FX reserves. We reattribute the dollar-backed part of the ECU as USD and drop the gold-backed ECUs off our statistics as gold is not foreign exchange.

blocks.head: 2) Computation of Constant Exchange Rate (CER) based shares.
blocks.text: Change in valuation of currencies affects shares of each currency in FX reserves. When the yen falls against the dollar, the yen's share in global FX reserves drops even when FX reserve managers make no active decision in their portfolio. In order to remove this valuation effect, we re-compute shares with cross-currency exchange rates fixed at end-2025 exchange rates. The ECB publishes the euro's share of global FX reserves in the same manner in its annual report, The International Role of the Euro (ECB, 2026).

blocks.head: 3) Net change in shares excluding valuation effects.
blocks.text: We compute how the valuation change in each currency would move its share in the global FX reserves, and read the difference from the actual change as what reserve managers added or shed from their FX reserves. In 2022, for example, the dollar's appreciation alone would have raised its share by 1.8 points, but the share fell 0.5 points, implying managers shed about 2.2% of global FX reserves worth of USD that year. Not all of that is a change of view: a manager holding a currency to a fixed weight has to sell it once it has appreciated, simply to return to that weight, and across 1981-2025 a little over half of each year's valuation drift is traded back this way. Of the 2.2 points in the 2022 example, roughly 1 point is that mechanical rebalancing and the rest a genuine shift in allocation. These series are best read as a record of trades rather than of decisions. These estimates strip out exchange-rate effects only; reinvested interest income stays inside them. Our year-by-year decomposition follows the approach of Arslanalp, Eichengreen and Simpson-Bell (2022).

references_html: ECB, The International Role of the Euro, 2026.
S. Arslanalp, B. Eichengreen & C. Simpson-Bell, “The Stealth Erosion of Dollar Dominance”, IMF Working Paper 22/58, 2022.

charts.title: US dollar: three measures of its share of world reserves
charts.note: The published series begins in 1995 and is the same as ours from 2000. The shaded band spans two treatments of the portion the IMF does not attribute to a named currency.
charts._series_order: The published series is listed LAST so it draws on top. From 2000 it and the JMA series are the same numbers, and in manifest order it was hidden beneath them — which read as the official series ending in 2000.
